question: Can God be tempted?
summary: James 1:13 declares God "cannot be tempted with evil" — a flat denial of divine temptability. Deuteronomy 6:16 (and Jesus citing it at Matt 4:7 / Luke 4:12) commands "Ye shall not tempt the Lord your God" — a command that presupposes God CAN be tempted, otherwise why forbid it? The verses contradict on whether God is subject to temptation at all.

reconcile.connective: Defenders resolve the tension by distinguishing two senses of "tempt": Deuteronomy means to test or provoke God, while James denies only that God can be enticed to evil.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells (Skeptic's Annotated Bible) presses the row directly: the very command "do not tempt God" would be pointless if, as James says, God simply cannot be tempted at all.

pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage directly, resolving it by noting 'temptation' has two grand meanings — solicitation to sin (James's sense) versus trial from circumstances (the Deut/Massah sense).

excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke states the harmonization's core move explicitly: 'temptation' carries two senses, so James (entice-to-sin) and the Deut/Massah usage (trial/providential) are not denying the same thing. Truncated mid-sentence with the elision marker.
excerpts.source_note_text: Let no man say - Lest the former sentiment should be misapplied, as the word temptation has two grand meanings, solicitation to sin, and trial from providential situation or circumstances, James, taking up the word in the former sense, after having used it in the latter, says: Let no man say, when he is tempted, (solicited to sin), I am tempted of God; for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he (thus) any man. Thus the author has explained and guarded his meaning.
